title: Is using AI as a tool really that different from artists taking inspiration from existing work?
author: santigv1500
selftext: Lately I’ve seen a lot of people say AI art is wrong because it’s trained on other people’s work. I get the concern, but at the same time… haven’t artists and devs always learned from what already exists, mixed influences, and made something new out of it? I’m not saying it’s exactly the same, obviously there are differences, but I do think there’s a big gap between soulless AI slop and actually using AI as a tool with intention, direction, and your own vision. Curious where other indie devs draw the line.

comments.author: CSEliot
comments.body:
It's about the consent. When you make art and share it, 5 years ago we all had the safe assumption of anything and everything pir art could be used for. Including as inspiration. 

Never written yet inherently known and agreed upon as a function of living in a society. 

99% of the population of the world had no idea these tools were being built back before they started to go public in 2022/2023.

The training and publication of these tools broke an international social contract that's been around for as long as humans have lived. 

It was done without anyones knowledge, hence the early models having watermarks in their generations. 

"But nobody is making money off of this"
Oh I promise you plenty are. The scientists, corpo officers, Nvidia, Oracle, and more. 

"But if artists knew about this, the technology wouldn't exist"
And? Journey before destination, friend. The path to unleashing your creativity side isn't somehow better just because you can turn your text into pixels that previously required much skill and training.

I draw the line at the point where a creative person and their personality is replaced by something cold and only caring for the output.

Of course that's frustrating, but does that make their work less valuable? I mean, photography didn't stop being art because you no longer needed to paint a portrait, and digital artists don't need to know how to mix physical paints. comments.author: Psychological-Key-36
comments.body:
I am an artist so you take what Id like to say with skepticism if this suits you.   
I make graphics for Minecraft mods and 100% of my work for mods is open source and I’m happy with anyone taking my work and turn it anyway they want. You can feed it to an AI to train or steer it, I don’t care, that is good for you if you can make a mod reusing my assets.   
I also paint digital art occasionally, specifically faces of people I have love or have profound affection for. I’m against AI feeding off of these, and not against human people taking inspiration. Artists have a different relationship to each of their piece of art and I believe I should be able to consent or not consent to AI training on this specific work. I have nothing against AI and I use it everyday.   
Yes, using AI as a tool differs from artists taking inspiration, we bond over emotions and intention through artistic expression.   
One artist taking inspiration because they liked what they saw is different than a robot absorbing your entire gallery for the sake of generating averaged out pieces of art. There is art that I make that I will allow being industrialized to train the robot overlord and art that is deeply personal that I don’t want being processed by a cold emotionless machine.   
I’m also not against being told I’m wrong or biased if yall think I am but I’d rather interesting replies than straight up downvotes

I still see AI as a useful creative tool, but I can definitely understand your perspective, especially when it comes to art that has a personal meaning to you.

comments.author: Prestigious_Edge_472
comments.body:
Do whatever you see fit, as long as you put in the effort into producing something good and not just prompt and accept whatever comes out the other end IMO. You're deifnitely allowed to do the latter, but if you produce garbage then don't expect anyone to like it, AI or not.  
  
People will yell and scream about consent for art, but there is no consent for knowledge, code, human like writing, translation or any other data that AI companies absorbed and trained their models on.  
  
Is it ethical? definitely not, but it's already done with the majority of the content out there on the web and it is clear that it will not stop/be stopped anytime soon.   
  
I think a major part of the uproar is about indie devs who don't want the competition from 'vibe coders' since they're mostly scared about their games being buried by the mass production of shovelware/AI slop as it's called now adays and artists who are worried about losing their job/sense of self. (There is a point to their fears as AI is causing waves in every field it enters and is causing job insecurity and changing the workflow of most professions it touches)  
  
Keep in mind, assets flip/shovelware/copies/clones were the previous 'AI slop', so there will always be something for people to rile up about.

One thing note mentioning, the majority of what I've seen from AI assets creation appear to be mostly advertising and has no basis in reality, AI assets creation lag behind considerably and still requires a human in the loop to do manual clean-up or to implement certain steps.

It's one thing to be against AI from an ethical point of view as a whole, it's a whole other thing where you decide what is ok to be AI and what isn't based on your own moral views and stance.

comments.author: Jolly-Rip5973
comments.body:
Yes & No

The greatest artists come up with something new that people have never seen before, most of the really famous artists came up with a somewhat unique or specialized style.

The really great artists were actually responsible for creating new art styles even.

If you look at artists like Dali, Georgia O'keeffe, Frank Frazetta, Boris Vallejo, Michael Whelan, Gerald Brom, they are not simply copying reality. They embellishing reality and adding their own artistic vision and taste to make something unique.

When you use Ai you are basically just mixing together things which have already been done and various artist's style of been highly blended together to create something which is sort of a generic default version of what you prompt for. This is what makes AI art look like Ai. 

In the real art world, there are 1000s of nuanced in actual oil paintings which each individual artist contributes to his unique works. A ChatGPT image prompted for an oil painting gives you a generic ChatGPT oil painting look.

If you get into using open source models and you learn to train LORA files, you can train the Ai models to bend that generic look into something with more nuance though.

There is a huge difference between an artists with a unique artistic vision using Ai as a tool and someone with no artistic vision, letting the AI model provide the artistic vision for them.

There are specialized types of artists like "character design artists" that have studied how to create unique interesting characters and they put a great deal of thought into their creations. They usually give their characters unique quirks, backstories, iconic accessories, body shapes, hair styles, attire, etc. all coming together to give their characters a unique identity. This require a large amount of human thought going into the character design. This is quite different from someone prompting "1 girl, elf, ranger, leather armor".

Ai can be a tool for professional artists but it can also just be lazy, low thought, low effort affair that gives you something generic.

comments.author: kytheon
comments.body:
Is buying an iPhone with money the same as stealing it from the Apple Store? The result is the same: a new iPhone in your hand. No of course it's not the same.

But in the arguments with anti-AI people the trick is that the premise is already wrong. The ingredients of the argument.  
They basically say "AI was trained on data. Not all data was paid for. So AI stole data. So using AI is stealing."

The question is if training on scraped data is stealing. I doubt it, so the rest of the argument falls apart. 

They will then argue "so you think stealing is not a crime?" which is a different argument altogether.

In addition to that, the model was trained in so much data that pointing out one is difficult. Can you copy a Van Gogh? Yes. Can you copy his style? Yes, but that's different. If you make any painting, and you ever looked at a Van Gogh before, did you copy him?

comments.author: AsparagusOk8818
comments.body:
most artists have no idea what the fckn machine does and refuse to learn. they hear about data scraping and basically assume that the machine is just copying their work, and ergo copyright should protect them. this is not what the machine does, and copyright laws suck ass and have never helped artists 

i am exhausted with terrible arguments from panicked artists who insist that the machine will destroy their market share, when in reality what the machine will do is reduce demand for artist work - which means they will have to price their work competitively, just like everyone else 

  
however 

  
no, the machine is not being 'inspired' by artwork. it is not the same thing. these are statistical models that exist in a world of math and probability. that's why they seem so smart - because humans are awful at understanding statistics and probability. but, to the machine, probability is a neatly signposted landscape - and that landscape opens the door to all kinds of possibilities 

what the machine does when it digests a piece of art is it adds that information to it's probability landscape. so when you query it to draw something, it goes to that area and looks up the most probable 'correct' answer to the query. this is why things are still so weird with visual art and writing, whereas coding and music have been effectively solved so fast - it's harder to say what a 'correct' way to write is or the 'correct' way to draw is. but music is much more mathematical, even if it is still subjective, and code is basically pure math 

it's why copyrighted works and characters can be immediately recalled with such high fidelity - there IS a correct way (more or less) to draw Darth Vader. at least the traditional image of Darth Vader. so it's easy to tokenize those parts of culture

likewise with extremely distinctive artistic styles. anything that you could comfortably give an empirical grading to in terms of accuracy 

  
when i look at Van Gogh's 'Wheatfield With Crows' and feel my soul fracture, that's inspiration. that's not what the machine does. the machine attempts to catalogue the painting as statistical data: ok, that's a wheatfield; ok, that's crows; okay, that's Van Gogh's style; ok, this is an oil painting; ok, this is the specific painting 'Wheatfield With Crows'; etc 

that process of tokenization is how you get billions of parameters and model weights

the stable diffusion process can then be used to translate those tokens into an actual visualization via literal noise

  
trying to lay copyright over any of that process, even what may seem egregious, is a real hazard because... what do you own? the statistical territory surrounding the idea of Darth Vader? we don't even know what that fckn statistical territory is or how the fckn machine even WORKS on a fundamental level, because the big models have emergent properties that are currently beyond our understanding (which is just to say that when you scale a model up - make it large - it suddenly begins developing entirely new capabilities) 

so courts have been extremely reluctant to award any ownership claims (thank God) and litigation has largely orbited the illegal means by which some training data was acquired (pirating books, stealing sheet music, bypassing the NYT paywall...). so when an idiot says that courts have said tokenizing anything is a copyright violation, no, that person is an idiot. courts have been consistently awarding damages for piracy and theft that facilitated LLM training, NOT the outcomes of that training 

  
it isn't clear to me going forward how traditional ideas of copyright and IP are going to survive. the big media companies are clearly eager to sign licensing deals with the LLMs, and that will keep a deep moat around really high priced IP (like Star Wars), with the license can be enforced via de facto control rather than courts. but it's not clear what anyone outside of those moats are supposed to do

like, if you write a book, and I then tokenize your book... I've basically just circumvented your copyright without copying anything at all. because now I can recreate the overall style and tone of the book without ever mentioning the things an author would typically cite as a copyright violation (characters, places, specific plagiarized passages, etc). i can boil down the real substance of a work without interacting with the content of it at all 

right now, that kind of tokenization is half-baked at best. but it probably won't be forever, and it probably will eventually become trivial

replies.author: AsparagusOk8818
replies.body:
SOME qualities of art can be expressed through probabilities and statistics

but there is no way to statistically reproduce Van Gogh feeling like his whole world was crumbling and so he painted the most haunting image of a field ever made 

color choice, composition, accuracy of subject matter, aspect ratio, the surface level aesthetic choices of a style... all of that can be quantized as a token. but that tokenization process inherently has no continuity or story behind it

this is the one grievance artists have that i do fully agree with - there is something empty about a piece of art where if you try to explore it, there is no story or history. just tokenized data 

now, there can in fact still be a richness of story, because people are still making the art just in a different way... but there doesn't have to be anymore. it's easy to see a future, IMHO, where the machine can make something that stirs the emotions as much as the best paintings can... and you care to look deeper, and there is nothing deeper, because it was a piece just slopped out carelessly but created beautifully 

maybe meaning can be derived from the meta-narrative at that point, IDK 

worse than that is the idea that i could pervert your work and/or steal something truly intimate from you via tokenization and you have no recourse. like, maybe you write a song that was inspired by something like the loss of a child or a failing marriage, and it resonates with people and becomes popular. i tokenize that song - not the lyrics, not even the meter - but just the same statistical noise that is the invisible structure of the song, and i just pocket that and call it mine 

that's the future we're walking towards right now and artists in denial of the reality are going to be slapped in the face by it, IMHO

comments.author: DirectionBusiness483
comments.body:
It depends on the perspective. 

For a lot of people the "journey" is meaningful, not just the result.

If you're heavily using AI for art and can't program- saying "I made this" to the end-user or consumer is probably fairly accurate. But a lot of people, especially artists, are going to care about the process and origin. You played art director and writer, you didn't "make" it the same way they use that word. So it creates friction. You're not using words the same way.

So to them it feels like there's this "fraudulent" work being put out, and there's a clear difference between "someone put the time and effort into understanding and practicing my style in order to make art similar to my style through a combination of skill, effort, and appreciation" and "someone asked an AI to remake my stuff and a fairly effortless 1:1 without understanding or attribution is created".

I think it's really easy to understand that perspective.

Putting my work out with the understanding someone may love it and appreciate it enough to want to put effort into learning how I did it and copying it is just a different beast than "my work ended up as training data and now a 12 year old can recreate it".

We value creativity and effort and shared experiences.

comments.author: Misery_101
comments.body:
I've seen it come down to honesty and ethics. You have to understand the art community and people who actually commission artists and all that

I know this is about gamedev, and not commisons but I think its relevant for the same reason

Look at an art drama video from 6 years ago about tracers, then look at one about AI art today.

There are people who will prompt AI and then say they drew it, and essentially defraud people avoiding AI art. But they go to such great lengths to do this with fake speed paints and by tracing the AI art etc.

Its not really as controversial if someone uses AI in their workflow if its disclosed. Imo if you use it for references that you just cannot find I don't see the problem. If you trace over it. Well you're just as bad as a tracer.

But its the dishonest people that are the same people who would have been tracers before Gen AI that give it a bad rep. 

Just like how a company isnt going to want to hire someone who can only promot AI without fixing its mistakes, nobody wants to commission someone for $500 and then basically cannot get a consistent style.

Alot of people think GenAi can replicate styles well but the artifacts are so easy to spot if you have any art training. Its the same as a 10x engineer looking at vibecoded slop.

As somone else mentioned, AI is a statistical machine, it doesnt have human descion making, and you arent really going to get hyper specific never before seen art in consistently rendered styles and make hyper specific changes easily. Which every commission will have edits.

There's layers to this far beyond the end result if you want to learn about this, look up things like "Artist caught using AI" on YouTube and there are some really detailed drama pieces. 

I've been successful using AI in coding and it actually helping me (still not as good as if I did it myself but pretty good in broad strokes when I already know what I need, saves hours of typing and formatting) but as I actually learn art, id compare it to having a computer play a game for you and you just... watch. Like take the controller and play yourself. 

Art is far more than the end result.
